Summary  
Data source overview: The abstract describes EfficientZero, a MuZero-based, model-based reinforcement-learning algorithm that attains super-human Atari performance with only 100 k environment steps, dramatically improving sample efficiency compared with previous approaches. The paper frames the key practical risk for RL—excessive data requirements that hinder real-world deployment—and presents theoretical justifications, design decisions, implementation details, and empirical results that culminate in the EfficientZero intervention.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[83]  
Instruction-set improvement: The present instructions work, but asking extractors to cite “closest preceding section titles” is hard when sources lack section headers (e.g., abstracts). Allow citing “Abstract” or paragraph numbers. Providing a brief, machine-readable list of allowed edge verbs and examples would reduce edge-type variability. Finally, giving a numeric guideline for minimum/maximum nodes relative to source length (rather than a 5 k-word heuristic) would avoid over- or under-extraction for very short texts.

Inference strategy justification: The abstract alone gives limited detail; moderate inference (edge confidence 2) was used only to articulate implicit causal links (e.g., why model-based planning lowers sample complexity). All descriptions remain faithful to stated claims or standard MuZero literature.

Extraction completeness explanation: All explicit reasoning steps—from the top-level risk (high sample complexity) through mechanism, insight, design, implementation, empirical validation, to the proposed actionable intervention (training with EfficientZero)—are represented. Every node participates in at least one edge, forming a single connected fabric.

Key limitations:  
1. Only a short abstract was available; richer methodological nuances and alternative interventions that might appear in the full paper could not be captured.  
2. Validation evidence is limited to headline benchmark numbers; statistical rigor is unknown, lowering confidence scores.  
3. The intervention maturity is estimated (proof-of-concept) because deployment beyond academic benchmarks is not shown.
